runs.t: •  Ask and answer Have you ever…?
•  Ask a follow-up in the simple past
•  Tell a classmate about one experience

slides.notes:
Welcome learners as they arrive. Tonight is the first night of Level 4.
Point to the title and read it: "Have you ever…?" Say: "Tonight we get to know our classmates: places, foods, jobs, and things we've tried."
Read the three lines under "Today you will". Give one quick example of each: "Have you ever seen snow? Yes, I have." • "When did you see it? How was it?" • "I've run a race. I ran it in 2023. It was exciting."
Learners choose what to share. Places, foods, and jobs are always safe topics. Never ask how or when learners came to the U.S. Invented answers are fine in every activity.

Every goal is a good goal.
I can ask a follow-up in the past (
When did you…? How was it?

slides.notes:
Read each goal slowly. Learners repeat.
Goal 1: Have you ever seen snow? Goal 2: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. / No, never. I've never ridden a horse. Goal 3: When did you go there? How was it?
Goal 4: the experience, when, how it was. Goal 5: learners write a short introduction email to you (5–8 sentences) in Read & Write.
"We check at 7:22" = the Can-Do Self-Check. It is not a test grade. This page comes back in Weeks 8 and 15.

slides.notes:
Step 1 · 6:00–6:08 · Welcome, orientation, and Opening Talk · 8 min. Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio with 15 learners; 3–4 pairs with 7–8).
Before class, write on the board: Welcome! Level 4 · 6:00–7:30 · Break 6:45 · Homework every week (15–20 minutes) and the question What did you do last weekend?
Welcome and orientation (2 min, first): say your name and write it on the board. Show the workbook: "This is your book for tonight. Every week has the same parts." Point to the times on the board. Say: "We speak English in class. It's OK to make mistakes. Mistakes help us learn." Give out name tags.
Model with one learner: you ask, "What did you do last weekend?" The learner answers. Help them add a reason and a detail: "I went to the park. I went because it was sunny. My kids played soccer." Then you ask a follow-up: "How was it?" (Click to show the follow-up.)
Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in 3 sentences (the answer, a reason, a detail); A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card. The cards are on the next slide.
If behind: one card only.

slides.title: Listening C

runs.t: Hear it: gonna = going to, wanna = want to
Say it: the weak, short have
= want to: fine in everyday talk.
find things we have in common.

slides.notes:
"Hear it, say it" (3 min). Point to the script lines. gonna = going to: "Tonight we're going to find things we have in common." wanna = want to: "I want to go camping."
Say: "People often say gonna and wanna. This listening uses going to and want to."
Then practice the weak, short have (it sounds like "h'v"): Have you ever seen snow? and the contraction: I've never ridden a horse. The class repeats the two lines twice.
Everyday English: people often say gonna (going to) and wanna (want to). Learners will hear them often. They are fine in casual talk; in writing, at a job interview, or in a formal email, use going to and want to. The listening uses the full forms.

runs.t: I've ridden a horse. She's never flown.
(in 2015, last year, when I was ten)
I rode a horse in 2015. She flew to Texas last year.

slides.notes:
Box 4: which one? No time or a time. Each click shows one row.
Questions and answers (2 min): Q: Can I say I have seen snow in 2022? A: No. With a finished time, use the simple past: I saw snow in 2022. • Q: Why eaten, not eat? A: After have / has, use the past participle: Have you ever eaten sushi? Look at Box 3. • Q: How do I answer Have you ever…? short? A: Yes, I have. or No, I haven't. or No, never. Then add a detail in the past: Yes, I have. I went there in 2022.
Check questions: "I have seen snow in 2022. Right or wrong?" (wrong: I saw snow in 2022.) • "Have you ever eat sushi? Right or wrong?" (wrong: eaten) • "She's lived in three cities. She's = she is or she has?" (she has).
Lesson plan: Step 4; Grammar Box 4; Questions and answers.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:15 · Talk Time: Find Someone Who Has… + Two True, One Invented · 15 min.
Model it first (1 min): take the sheet and ask one learner, "Have you ever flown in a plane?" When they say yes, ask two follow-ups: "When did you fly? How was it?" Write their name on your sheet. Say: "Two follow-ups. Then write the name."
Round 1 (7 min): Find Someone Who Has… (mingle). Learners stand with the Talk Time sheet and ask classmates. When someone says Yes, they ask two follow-ups in the past (When? Where? How was it?) and write the name and a short note. One name per classmate, then move on. Each click shows the next step.
15 learners: whole-room mingle. 7–8 learners: mingle in one circle. 5 or fewer: one group; each person asks every other person 2 prompts.
Baseline snapshot (during Talk Time): listen to about 5 learners for 1 minute each. For each one, note: 3 connected sentences? a follow-up question? any present perfect? This is not a test; don't tell learners a score. Keep the notes private.
